awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Functionally Graded Nickel/Titanium-Based Shape Memory Alloys and Devices with Tunable Properties
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on the development of advanced materials and devices that can actively respond to changes in temperature, mechanical stress, and environmental conditions. By using a specialized 3D printing process, this technology enables precise control over the local properties of metallic components. The approach creates materials with tailored responses within a single, seamless component, eliminating the need for complex assemblies or extensive finishing processes. The adaptable materials and devices have the potential to benefit industries such as healthcare, aerospace, automotive, and energy, by providing reliable, compact, and customizable solutions. For instance, this technology can improve medical implants for spinal surgeries, reducing surgical invasiveness and enhancing patient outcomes, and can create robust pipe couplers that replace less reliable connections currently used in aerospace, automation, and oil and gas industries. 

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of functionally-graded shape memory alloys featuring precise local chemical compositions, microstructure, and mechanical behavior. The solution leverages a controlled evaporation phenomenon during the laser powder bed fusion 3-D printing process, allowing exact control of certain elemental concentrations within shape memory alloys. This precision enables the deliberate adjustment of solid-state phase transformations and mechanical properties, achieving tailored superelasticity, thermal actuation temperatures, and tunable stiffness within a single component. Unlike existing manufacturing approaches, this method avoids extensive post-processing and complex component assembly, offering scalable and reproducible material behavior across a wide temperature range. The technology provides enhanced reliability, reduced component complexity, and better multifunctionality.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The major goal of this NSF I-Corps project was to explore the commercialization potential of functionally graded NiTi-based shape memory alloys (SMAs) and devices developed through prior NSF-supported research, and to provide entrepreneurial training to the project team through structured customer discovery. The underlying technology uses additive manufacturing (AM), particularly laser-based metal AM, to control local alloy chemistry, microstructure, transformation temperatures, and mechanical response within a single metallic component. At the start of the project, the team considered a broad range of potential applications, including large-scale pipe couplings for oil and gas systems, biomedical implants, aerospace actuators, automotive thermal-control components, and robotic devices. The I-Corps effort was therefore focused on identifying which application represented the clearest customer need and the most practical route to commercialization.

During the regional and national I-Corps activities, the team conducted approximately 100 structured customer interviews across upstream, midstream, and downstream oil and gas organizations, original equipment manufacturers, engineering and procurement organizations, utilities, materials and manufacturing companies, and other technical stakeholders. The customer discovery process substantially refined the original commercialization hypothesis. Interviews showed that several initially considered upstream applications were limited by field accessibility, established connection practices, qualification requirements, and the difficulty of introducing a new coupling technology into downhole or highly constrained systems. In contrast, operators, integrity engineers, maintenance personnel, and industrial partners repeatedly identified a more immediate need in above-ground pressurized piping systems, where welding and mechanically preloaded repair systems impose significant operational burdens. Welding is reliable but can require system shutdown, ignition-risk controls, certified labor, surface preparation, and inspection. Mechanical clamps and related non-welded solutions can reduce installation time, but customers expressed concerns regarding preload relaxation, installation variability, sealing stability, and long-term confidence under pressure and thermal cycling.

As a result of these findings, the project narrowed the commercial focus from a broad functionally graded SMA platform to a specific product direction: a permanent, weld-free SMA pipe joining and reinforcement system for above-ground industrial piping. The value proposition was refined around faster installation, reduced dependence on welding, lower downtime and safety exposure, tolerance to real-world geometric variation, and stable, self-adjusting contact pressure over time. The customer discovery process also clarified the stakeholder and decision-making structure. Maintenance technicians are directly affected by installation complexity; integrity and materials engineers evaluate technical acceptability and repair methods; operations managers and asset owners are strongly influenced by downtime, safety, and lifecycle reliability; and engineering, procurement and construction firms, pipe or connector manufacturers, and service providers can serve as important commercialization and qualification partners. The project generated concrete translational outputs including a refined Business Model Canvas, stakeholder map, interview database, clearer market segmentation, and a customer-informed technical development roadmap.

The intellectual merit of the project was reflected in the transition from a materials-centered innovation to an application-defined engineering solution. The team identified additive manufacturing as a key enabler for overcoming the scale and manufacturability limitations that have historically restricted SMA couplers. In addition to enabling near-net-shape fabrication of large SMA components, AM provides the ability to spatially program transformation behavior within a monolithic coupler. This capability can be used to create multi-stage engagement, distribute contact pressure more gradually, reduce sensitivity to local tolerances, and maintain joint performance without relying on uniform bolted preload or a single sharp actuation event. Customer feedback directly informed the technical requirements that must be demonstrated before industrial adoption, including repeatable actuation, stable contact pressure, leak tightness, resistance to axial slip, tolerance to pipe ovality and surface condition, predictable response under temperature and pressure variations, practical installation procedures, and a credible qualification pathway. These findings directly informed the follow-on NSF Translation to Practice - Translation (TTP-T) proposal submitted by the team to develop and validate demonstration-ready SMA pipe couplers for industrial piping systems.

The project also produced important broader impacts. The I-Corps experience trained the Technical Lead, Entrepreneurial Lead, and Industry Mentor in evidence-based entrepreneurship, customer discovery, market segmentation, value-proposition development, stakeholder mapping, and commercialization planning. It strengthened the team's ability to translate advanced materials research into customer-defined engineering requirements and created sustained engagement with operators, OEMs, service companies, and commercialization partners. If successfully developed and deployed, the resulting weld-free SMA joining technology has the potential to improve worker safety by reducing ignition-related welding activities, shorten installation and repair times, reduce costly industrial downtime, and improve long-term reliability of critical piping infrastructure. The project did not produce publications directly under the I-Corps award; its principal outcomes were market validation, customer and stakeholder discovery, refinement of the commercial application, and definition of the technical and translational pathway required for continued development and commercialization.
